election._note: D'Hondt in a single national constituency with a 3% threshold, waived for national-minority lists -- national PR in the plainest sense, the waiver unmodelled. Elected 17 December 2023 for four years, so the next is due by December 2027; an earlier snap election has been repeatedly floated and is the dissolution rule's to price. Constitution of Serbia, Art. 100; Wikipedia, '2023 Serbian parliamentary election'.

dissolution._note: The President dissolves the Assembly on the Government's reasoned proposal (Art. 109) -- an executive-advice shape the parliamentary_republic template reads as self_dissolution, MLT's precedent. Snap elections in 2014, 2016, 2020 and 2023 show the lever is used; elections follow within 45-60 days. Constitution of Serbia, Art. 109.

head_of_state._note: The President, directly elected for five years, two terms at most; elected April 2022, so the next falls in April 2027. Formally limited, in practice the dominant figure of the governing party -- an informal power the parliamentary template cannot express and records here instead. Constitution of Serbia, Arts. 114-116.
head_of_state.title: President

amendment._note: Art. 203: two thirds of all deputies; amendments to the preamble, the principles, rights and freedoms, the system of authority, states of emergency and the amendment procedure itself then go to a mandatory referendum. The machinery carries the two_thirds bar; the mandatory-referendum tier is read as optional, recorded below. Constitution of Serbia, Art. 203.
amendment._referendum_note: Art. 203(7): the entrenched chapters need a referendum by law, the rest do not -- a split the referendum field cannot carry, so the softer reading is authored. Constitution of Serbia, Art. 203.
amendment._permits_system_change_note: No eternity clause; the 2006 constitution replaced the 1990 one by the referendum route, and the system of authority sits inside the amendable, referendum-gated tier.

judicial._note: A Constitutional Court reviews the constitutionality of laws (Arts. 166-175). Constitution of Serbia, Art. 167.

formation._note: The President proposes a Prime Minister after consulting the lists, and the Assembly elects the government by a majority of all deputies (Art. 127). A no-confidence vote needs a majority of all deputies (Art. 130); the template's simple_present is the nearest bar. The current Prime Minister took office in April 2025 after his predecessor resigned. Constitution of Serbia, Arts. 127, 130.

government._pretender_note: Whom data/laws/amendments.json's Restoration Act puts on the throne. Serbia was a kingdom until 1918 and its crown passed into Yugoslavia's; the restored monarch here is fictional.

fiscal._note: General government, IMF/Ministry of Finance ~2024, rounded, on AUT.json's conventions. VAT 20% standard; corporate 15%; income 10% is the statutory flat wage tax, with social contributions (~35% of gross) carrying most of the labour burden through revenue rather than this rate; capital gains 15%; no wealth tax. Revenue ~38% of GDP includes social contributions. Debt ~47% of GDP (end-2024). Infrastructure 4.5% reflects the capital-spending programme of the mid-2020s. Spending scaled to expenditure near 43% of GDP.
